title: 46. Investigating two methods of lidocaine administration for pain mitigation during band castration in lambs.
content:
Abstract
Castration is a common livestock management practice used to control reproduction and prevent unwanted behaviors from intact males. Band castration is a common method, yet, it is known to induce acute stress and discomfort, prompting animal welfare concerns. Lidocaine can be used to provide local anesthesia; however, access, administration route, technician confidence, and effectiveness may influence its adoption. Thus, the objective of this study was to investigate the efficacy of two lidocaine application methods during band castration. Sixteen lambs were randomly assigned to no castration (CON; n = 3), castration with a lidocaine impregnated band (LB; n = 7), or castration with lidocaine injection and standard band (LI; n = 6). Behavioral observations, mechanical nociceptive thresholds (MNT) via algometry, and surface temperature via infrared thermography were collected at -1d, 0h, 1h, 6h, 12h, 24h, 3d, and 7d relative to banding. Bodyweight and average daily gain (ADG) were collected for the first 12d of life. Growth by weight and ADG did not differ by treatment, but bodyweight increased (P < 0.05) over time, and twins had greater (P < 0.05) ADG and weight gain compared to triplets. There was a treatment x time effect in which LI lambs had a lower (P < 0.05) scrotal MNT at 0h compared to CON lambs, and LB lambs did not differ from either. Conversely, 1h after banding LI lambs had a greater (P < 0.05) scrotal MNT compared to LB lambs, while neither differed from CON. Triplet lambs had a greater (P < 0.05) scrotal MNT compared to twins. A treatment x time interaction was also observed for surface temperature below band placement in which at -1d, temperatures were lower (P < 0.05) in CON lambs compared to LI and LB lambs, which did not differ. However, at 7d temperatures were lower (P < 0.05) below the band in LI and LB lambs compared to CON lambs. Surface temperatures below the band did not differ by birth type. A treatment x time effect for temperature above the band indicated that at -1d, 6h, 12h, 24h and 3d temperatures were lower (P < 0.05) in CON lambs compared to LI and LB lambs, which did not differ. At 0h and 1h LI lambs had higher (P < 0.05) surface temperatures above the band compared to CON, while LB lambs did not differ from LI or CON. Surface temperatures were greater (P < 0.05) above the band in twins compared to triplets. Visual analog scores and vocalization frequencies immediately after banding did not differ between groups or by birth type. These data suggest that lidocaine injection may be more effective at mitigating the acute pain response compared to lidocaine bands, but both methods are effective after the first hour post banding.
